thread.title_full: Montana State awarded $10.7 million to expand biomedical research and workforce development

author: big sky times
title: Montana State awarded $10.7 million to expand biomedical research and workforce development
text:
Montana State University announced on May 20 that it has received $10.7 million from the National Institutes of Health to establish a new center aimed at strengthening biomedical research, workforce development, and public health in Montana.
The funding will be used to create the Center for Advanced Molecular Pathogenesis (CAMP), which is designed to help early-career scientists develop independent research programs and build infrastructure for scientific discovery. The award comes through the NIH Centers of Biomedical Research Excellence program, which invests in states like Montana to increase research capacity and access to innovation.
Over five years, CAMP will provide mentorship, research support, and shared scientific resources so faculty can compete for federal grants and develop sustainable programs. “This is an investment in people and in Montana’s future,” said Alison Harmon, vice president for research and economic development at MSU. “By building research capacity here, we’re creating new opportunities for students, strengthening our ability to address health challenges and expanding the state’s role in biomedical discovery.”
CAMP is led by Blake Wiedenheft, Winifred Asbjornson Plant Sciences Endowed Chair and professor; Jovanka Voyich, professor and department head; both from the Department of Microbiology and Cell Biology in the College of Agriculture; along with partners across campus. A central feature is the Advanced Biological Imaging and Cell Analysis Core that will offer technologies such as cryo-electron microscopy as well as technical expertise accessible statewide.
The center will initially support three faculty members focusing on infectious disease: Alyssa Evans (Microbiology & Cell Biology), Heather Callaway (Microbiology & Cell Biology/Chemistry & Biochemistry), and Madison Collins (Biological & Physical Sciences at MSU Billings). Their projects include studying how viruses invade nervous systems or are recognized by immune responses for vaccine design as well as examining human immune reactions against antibiotic-resistant bacteria like MRSA.
“Programs like CAMP help ensure that the next generation of scientists can build their careers in Montana,” Wiedenheft said. “By investing in people and shared scientific infrastructure, we’re creating a foundation for discoveries that improve public health and expand opportunity across the state.” Co-director Voyich added: “That kind of legacy is exactly what inspires the work we’re building at MSU… It allows us to create the kind of supportive environment where scholars can build successful careers providing the resources they need to pursue big ideas.”
Montana State University leads in research funding within Montana with annual expenditures exceeding $288 million according to its official website. The university enrolls about 17,165 students split between residents and nonresidents; it also ranks among top global universities per rankings cited by its official website. As Montana’s land-grant institution focused on education, outreach, volunteer efforts, community service initiatives—and serving both state residents as well as broader communities—MSU continues expanding its influence according to its official website.
